subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The First Car Race
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The First Car Race.

hook.text: In 1894, a French newspaper organized a race from Paris to Rouen—the first real car competition.

buildup.text: Over 100 entries applied, but only 21 cars actually started the 79-mile journey.

discovery.text: The winner averaged about 12 mph—barely faster than a horse but enough to prove a point.

twist.text: The judges disqualified the car that finished first because it needed a stoker to run its steam engine.

climax.text: The event turned automobiles from curiosities into competitive machines overnight.

punchline.text: The first car race was slower than a bicycle sprint.

quiz.question: Where was the first major car race held in 1894?

details.summary: The first organized automobile race took place in 1894 from Paris to Rouen, covering 79 miles to demonstrate the reliability of the new horseless carriage rather than simply determine the fastest vehicle.
details.whyItMatters: This event proved to a skeptical public that automobiles were practical transportation, not just novelties. It sparked public interest in cars and launched the entire motorsport industry.
takeaways: The Paris-Rouen race of 1894 covered 79 miles in about 6 hours
Judging emphasized reliability and ease of handling over pure speed
Both steam and gasoline cars competed, with gasoline winning favor

faq.question: Who won the first car race?
faq.answer: Count Jules-Albert de Dion arrived first in a steam car, but the prize went to Peugeot and Panhard-Levassor gasoline cars because judges valued practicality. The steam car required a stoker and was deemed impractical.

faq.question: How fast were cars in the first race?
faq.answer: The average speed was about 12 mph, a pace easily outrun by a decent cyclist. But covering 79 miles without horse power was remarkable for 1894 and captured the public imagination.
